newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Church attacks Brazil for neglect of Indians.
newsitem.headline: Church attacks Brazil for neglect of Indians.

text.p: The Brazilian Catholic Church blasted the government over its Indian policy on Wednesday, citing a sharp increase in the invasion of reservations and rising illness as evidence of negligence by the state.

"The government's policy is one of negligence on the most important issues for indigenous people, like hunger and the non-preservation of their lands," said Bishop Apparecido Jose Dias, president of the Indigenous Missionary Council (CIMI).
The bishop urged the government to complete the demarcation of Indian lands, which is years behind schedule, and improve health care in indigenous communities.

CIMI officials said the number of new invasions of Indian lands rose to 33 in the first 10 months of 1996, from 13 in 1995 as a whole, with logging companies and gangs of miners the main culprits. They also said 14,700 cases of illness were detected among a total indigenous population of about 320,000 in 1996, compared with 15,600 cases in 1994 and 1995 combined.
CIMI executive secretary Saulo Feitosa said the publication in January of a controversial government decree, which gives non-Indians the chance to claim Indian land, had encouraged land invasions.

Feitosa also accused the government was not taking simple steps to improve health among indigenous communities. He cited the case of the Deni tribe in Amazonas state whose population fell by 25 percent to 460 members between 1991 and 1995 after deaths from measles, tuberculosis and malaria.

"The statistics tend to show relative stability in categories like murder," Feitosa said. "What is alarming is the growth in violence caused by the negligence, and in some cases aggression, by the state."
A report published by the CIMI on Wednesday said 30 Indians were murdered by non-Indians in 1995, down from 45 in 1994 and 43 in 1993, but crime by Indians against Indians was rising.

The number of suicides rose to 58 in 1995 from 35 and 39 in the previous two years respectively, and 106,764 Indians, roughly one-third of the total population, were suffering from malnutrition, the report said.

"The phenomenom of self-destruction through suicide and crime within the Indian groups is clearly linked to pressures that result from the loss of land," CIMI legal adviser Rosane Lacerda said. "Perhaps this is the most effective method yet for their extermination."

Apparecido, who is bishop of Amazonian state of Roraima, urged the government to take urgent action to halt the spread of AIDS among the indigenous population. Official statistics show that 11 Indians have died of AIDS since 1989, while another four are HIV-positive.
